oneliner.t: Huntsville native, master plumber and mechanical-contracting business owner who won the June 16, 2026 Democratic runoff and is challenging Rep. Dale Strong on a government-reform platform; first run for office.

upbringing.t: Sneed grew up in Huntsville and graduated from Lee High School. In his Ballotpedia survey he says his first job (from summer 1995) was as a part-time lifeguard at Mountain Springs Pool, where he rose to head coach and manager by 2003, the year he earned a bachelor's degree from Boston University. His listed occupations include actor, stuntman, bartender, farmer and restaurant manager. He says he returned to Huntsville in 2012 to start a family, rose from a $10-an-hour helper to master plumber and HVAC contractor, and founded his own company in 2019, which he says now runs six trucks with eight workers. He says his late father taught him 'you have to like who you see in the mirror.' These details are his own account, not independently corroborated.

career.role: Plumbing helper to master plumber / HVAC

platform.t: 12-year congressional term limits; reverse Citizens United; ban members' trading of individual stocks; five-year wait before ex-lawmakers can lobby; enforceable Supreme Court ethics code.
Says Congress has ceded power and criticizes Strong for supporting expanded executive authority.
Repeal 'harmful tariffs' and change the tax code so the wealthy pay their fair share.
Restore the ACA subsidies; broader insurance reform.
Protect organized labor and 'the dignity of honest work'; reinvest in public education.
Supports same-day registration and universal mail-in voting; open to an Election Day holiday or multi-day voting.
Supports government regulation and monitoring of AI.

promises.t: Push 12-year term limits for House and Senate members.
Ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks.
Five-year lobbying ban for former lawmakers.
An enforceable ethics code for Supreme Court justices.

claims.claim: Rose from a $10-an-hour helper to master plumber and HVAC contractor; founded his company in 2019 and now runs six trucks and eight workers.

record.t: APR describes him as a plumber and small-business owner; state plumbing-board license and business records were not checked.

claims.claim: Outraised Rep. Strong in the latest FEC reporting period (second period in a row).

record.t: APR, citing FEC filings, reports Sneed $177,789.53 vs. Strong $125,570.65 for Apr. 30–June 30, 2026 (APR's 'more than $57,000' gap is overstated; the difference is about $52,219). The earlier period was not checked. Strong still had far more cash ($1.42M vs. $169,720 on June 30). The earlier period: Axios (Feb 10, 2026) noted reports that Sneed apparently outraised Strong in Q4 2025 but gave no quarterly figures, so the "second period" part is supported by reporting rather than checked against filings.

claims.claim: Takes no money from AIPAC, corporate PACs or dark-money groups; besides one $1,000 leadership-PAC gift, all contributions come from individuals.
claims.short: No AIPAC or corporate PAC money

record.t: FEC shows $2,350 from all non-party committees through June 30, 2026; Track AIPAC does not list him. The $2,350 is slightly more than the single $1,000 gift described — the remaining $1,350 is not itemized here.

claims.claim: Over 90% of his contributions come from inside the district.

record.t: No state/ZIP breakdown was retrieved. 1819 News reported that donations routed through ActBlue (a conduit for individual donors) made up over half of his itemized contributions as of June 2026, without a geographic breakdown.

claims.claim: Strong's campaign receives overwhelming support from corporations and PACs.

record.t: PACs gave $631,300 of Strong's $1,477,819 (43%) in 2025–26 per FEC; the corporate share of that isn't broken out. APR reported over 90% of his latest-quarter money came from PACs, lobbyists or executives.

claims.claim: More than 120 congressional candidates nationwide have signed his BAC Pledge.
Said Rep. Greg Landsman of Ohio became the first sitting member of Congress to endorse the BAC reform pledge.

record.t: No pledge roster or Landsman statement could be opened in this pass.

claims.claim: Says he spent about 25 years working with his hands before entering politics.

record.t: His own Ballotpedia survey lists lifeguarding from 1995, then work as an actor, stuntman, bartender, farmer and restaurant manager, and plumbing from 2012. That is broadly consistent with the claim, but it is his own account, with no independent employment or licensing record checked.

aipac_endorse.t: Not listed on Track AIPAC (as of 2026-10-08); says he takes no AIPAC money.

note.t: Candidate financial disclosure (House Clerk) not located or opened.

townhalls.note: Announced plans for a town hall in Jackson County (Aug. 2026); date and attendance not confirmed.

note.t: Huntsville native; lived away (Boston University, through about 2003, and elsewhere) and returned to Huntsville in 2012.

checks.claims: Mechanical sample could not use the campaign site (sneedforcongress.com unreachable). Used his Ballotpedia survey (bio claims, first issue statements) and his campaign statements as reported by APR and 256 Today. No ads found. 7 checkable claims rated (2 true, 1 partly, 4 unverifiable). Oct 8, 2026 pass: Campaign site unreachable again this pass: direct fetches were refused (the proxy blocked the domain, and the fetch tool only opens URLs that have already turned up in a search or fetch result), web.archive.org was blocked, and the shared web-search budget was used up before any new search could run. So the work was limited to pages already cited in this file or linked from them. Re-read his Ballotpedia survey; its first issue answers are policy positions (repeal tariffs, restore agency funding, restore ACA subsidies, the BAC pledge) rather than checkable facts. Added 2 claims from 256 Today. Now 9 claims: 2 true, 1 partly, 6 unverifiable. That is 3 with a checkable verdict.
checks.democracy: Never held office, so there are no certification votes. Oct 8, 2026: reviewed his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey (it backs same-day registration, universal mail voting and an Election Day holiday or multi-day voting, but says nothing about the 2020/2024 results) and coverage in 256 Today, APR, Axios (Feb and Jun 2026) and 1819 News. None contains a statement on the 2020 or 2024 results. A fresh news search could not run (search budget exhausted), so this is marked "news".
